HR@10 against 99 sampled negatives measures ranking within 100 candidates, not full-catalog top-10 retrieval. Krichene and Rendle show that sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; fixed candidates make comparisons reproducible but do not remove this bias. Thus, improvements support the pinned sampled benchmark, without establishing better full-catalog recommendations. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For this benchmark, one additional hit among 200 users changes category HR@10 by 0.005 and the four-category macro-average by 0.00125. A suitable paired bootstrap resamples users within each category, preserves each user’s baseline/proposal hit pair, and recomputes the macro-average difference. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fixed candidates and fitted models; it does not capture negative-sampling or training-seed uncertainty. Paired resampling follows established retrieval-comparison practice. [Statistical Significance Tests for IR Evaluation](https://ciir-publications.cs.umass.edu/getpdf.php?id=744)

Repeatedly selecting checkpoints and architectures on the same validation users creates selection optimism: the largest observed gain partly reflects favorable noise. An ordinary bootstrap interval computed after choosing the winner does not account for that adaptive search. Treat small gains as provisional, report per-category differences and paired intervals, record the search scope, and reserve claims of generalization for the untouched final evaluation under the prescribed protocol. [Cawley and Talbot, 2010](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
